title: Geometry of Noisy Quantum Many-Body Dynamics with Continuous Symmetries: Entanglement and Correlations
abstract: We study unitary quantum dynamics in noisy Brownian models with global continuous symmetries, such as $U(1)$ and $SU(2)$, focusing on Rényi entanglement entropies and hydrodynamic and non-hydrodynamic correlators. By mapping the averaged late-time dynamics to the low-energy physics of effective replica Hamiltonians, we find that the evolution is controlled by the quantum geometry of their ground-state manifolds, which is directly related to the geometry of $k$-commutants---the symmetry algebra of $k$ replicas of the system. In interacting systems, these $k$-commutants are generically determined solely by the symmetries of the system, independent of microscopic details of the noisy evolution. This allows us to use the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) to provide simple geometric explanations for the sub-ballistic Rényi entanglement growth and the anomalous decay of non-hydrodynamic correlators in interacting systems with continuous symmetries. We find this behavior to be intimately connected to singularities within the $k$-commutant manifolds, arising from frozen ``void'' states in the Hilbert space that exist due to continuous on-site symmetries. This also demystifies the important role of voids in the dynamics of these observables, previously identified in $U(1)$ symmetric systems. We compare these behaviors in interacting systems with Abelian and non-Abelian continuous symmetries and in free-fermion systems, which differ in the geometry of their $k$-commutants. Ultimately, this work provides a general geometric framework for systematically studying observables in noisy systems with continuous symmetries, including Haar-random circuits.
summary: This paper develops a general geometric theory to analyze the late-time dynamics of noisy quantum many-body systems with continuous symmetries. By mapping the evolution onto the geometry of $k$-commutant manifolds, it explains anomalous decay rates and entanglement growth using concepts from quantum geometry. This framework offers systematic tools for studying observables in complex, non-equilibrium settings.
main_problem: The study investigates unitary quantum dynamics in noisy many-body systems possessing global continuous symmetries, focusing on how entanglement and correlations evolve over time.
main_result: The late-time evolution is governed by the quantum geometry of effective $k$-commutant manifolds, providing a geometric explanation for sub-ballistic entanglement growth and anomalous correlator decay linked to manifold singularities.
method: The authors employ replica theory, mapping dynamics to low-energy physics on effective Hamiltonians, and utilize the Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP) adapted for singular ground state manifolds.
model_or_system: The analysis covers noisy Brownian models with continuous symmetries ($U(1), SU(2)$), generalized to interacting systems whose dynamics are characterized by $k$-commutant algebras. Specific toy models include the $es\eta$ model and free-fermion systems.
key_observables: Rényi entanglement entropies, hydrodynamic and non-hydrodynamic correlators, and the geometry of $k$-commutants.
important_parameters: The symmetry group ($U(1)$ vs. $SU(2)$), replica number ($k$), and system parameters defining the noise/interaction strength ($\lambda$, $\Delta$).
main_assumptions: Key challenges involve treating ground state manifolds that possess singularities, requiring extensions beyond standard smooth manifold dynamics treatments like TDVP.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but mention calculations involving overlaps and entropy scaling for specific models.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a review: Section II covers Brownian models; Section III characterizes $k$-commutant manifolds; Section IV applies TDVP to smooth systems (Heisenberg); Section V introduces singularity physics via toy models; Sections VI and VII address entanglement growth in $U(1)$ and $SU(2)$ symmetric systems, respectively.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful geometric framework for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex quantum systems, linking symmetry structure directly to observable scaling laws like entanglement entropy.
